title: Equipping L2 Teachers for Linguistic Justice in the Age of Generative AI: A Generative‐Curator Heuristic
abstract: ABSTRACT Although generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support second‐language (L2) teaching and learning through materials development, feedback, revisions, model texts and translation, generated language may also reproduce standard‐language, raciolinguistic and ableist norms. This conceptual article argues that existing AI literacy and teacher‐education frameworks do not yet fully address this language‐specific problem and offers a pedagogical heuristic to fill that gap. Drawing on AI literacy, critical digital literacy, language ideology, raciolinguistic and accessibility scholarship, we argue that L2 teachers should be prepared to be generative curators who critically select, adapt, contest, reject and redesign generated language while preserving learners’ agency, communicative purposes and linguistic repertoires. This heuristic is designed for pre‐service and in‐service L2 teacher education and focuses on the situated analysis of generated‐language artefacts, including feedback, revisions, model texts and translations. title: Emergent Bilingual Children's Translanguaging in a US Korean Church: Ethnographic Study
abstract: ABSTRACT This ethnographic study examines a Korean church in the US, focusing on the literacy, cultural engagement, and identity formation of emergent Korean‐English bilingual children. Grounded in translanguaging theory and ethnographic methodology, the study investigates how these children navigate Korean and English in church‐based Sunday school activities. Through observations and analysis of children's interactions, this study reveals how religious space facilitates the fluid use of linguistic repertoires and participation in cultural activities, fostering the development of language and cultural knowledge, and dynamic identity formation. The findings suggest that Korean churches can serve as dynamic sites where emergent bilinguals cultivate linguistic skills and a sense of their cultures, and further negotiate multifaceted identities, enhancing their sense of belonging within both their ethnic community and the wider global context. The study proposes a framework that conceptualizes religious space as a translanguaging space, encompassing languages, cultures, and identities.

What Contributes to Self‐Efficacy in Speaking Chinese as a Foreign Language: A Social Cognitive Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT Grounded in social cognitive theory, this study investigated how high‐evidence factors jointly contribute to Chinese‐as‐a‐foreign‐language (CFL) speaking self‐efficacy. Data from 236 CFL learners in Beijing revealed a multifaceted pattern of associations. Speaking strategy use and speaking motivation were positively associated with speaking self‐efficacy, whereas speaking anxiety showed a significant negative association. Classroom enjoyment, willingness to communicate (WTC), and communicative competence were associated with speaking self‐efficacy through indirect pathways involving strategy use, motivation, and anxiety. These findings highlight the layered and interconnected nature of cognitive, motivational, affective, behavioral, and environmental influences on CFL speaking self‐efficacy. By comparing a theory‐informed model with a non‐theoretical alternative, the study demonstrates the value of theoretically grounded modeling in yielding conceptually coherent and interpretable findings. title: ‘Whose Language Counts?’ Linguistic Racism, Gen‐AI, and Policy Silence in Polish and Romanian AI Governance
abstract: ABSTRACT As generative artificial intelligence spreads through European education, its development continues to be shaped overwhelmingly by English and other dominant languages. This article examines how national AI and digital education policies in Poland and Romania discursively construct a linguistically homogeneous ‘ideal learner,’ rendering Roma and refugee learners invisible in policy. Drawing on comparative critical discourse analysis of four national policy documents alongside three civil society reports, the analysis identifies three patterns: technocratic and economic nationalist discourse that presupposes linguistic homogeneity; rhetorical commitments to inclusion that erase linguistic diversity in practice; and the complete absence of guidance on linguistic variation in teacher preparation. Situating these dynamics within post‐socialist legacies of centralized linguistic governance, the article argues that AI governance operates as implicit language policy, and that treating it as such is a necessary condition for contesting the linguistic hierarchies these systems reproduce.

title: English Language Education in Rural Contexts: Examining Students’ Perceptions and Motivation Through a Contextually Grounded Extracurricular Program
abstract: ABSTRACT We conducted this case study in Türkiye to examine how a contextually grounded extracurricular program shaped rural students’ perceptions of English and their motivation to learn and use the language. Recognizing motivation as an equity‐related concern in rural contexts, where students may have limited opportunities to perceive the local relevance of English, we investigated a 4‐week program that connected English with students’ socioeconomic, sociocultural, and digital realities. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews and observation notes, we explored how students’ perceptions and motivation developed through the program. Before the program, the students viewed English as a global language associated with opportunities abroad and distant professional goals, while perceiving it as disconnected from everyday rural life. Their motivation was largely extrinsic, as they valued English mainly for its perceived educational and professional benefits. title: Mapping Multimodality in Translation Studies: A Systematic Review
abstract: ABSTRACT This systematic review examines recent developments in how multimodality has been conceptualised and investigated within translation studies, based on 113 articles identified through a search of 14 selected translation journals published between 2019 and 2024. Four main research foci were identified: modal transformation across media, spatial and multisensory contexts, audiovisual and accessibility‐oriented practices, and interpreting as multimodal mediation. These strands indicate that multimodality in translation studies has expanded beyond audiovisual translation (AVT) and contributed to a reconceptualisation of translation as a situated, embodied, and experiential practice. Methodologically, qualitative studies remain dominant in the dataset, whereas quantitative and mixed‐methods designs are less common and concentrated in particular research domains. The reviewed studies also draw mainly on two theoretical orientations: SFL‐informed social semiotic approaches and intersemiotic translation and resemiotisation. title: Finetuning Pre‐Trained Language Models for Automatic Assessment of English‐Chinese Interpreting
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent years have seen growing interest in leveraging pre‐trained language models (PLMs) for automatic assessment of spoken‐language performance. Contributing to this emerging line of work, the present study offers the first attempt to finetune two PLMs, GTE‐multilingual and mmBERT, for assessing English‐Chinese interpreting, using over 1700 human‐scored renditions rated on a four‐band, eight‐point analytic rubric. The models were trained using five‐fold cross‐validation to perform band‐level classification and point‐based score prediction, and were evaluated on a held‐out test set. Performance was assessed using multiple metrics, including Accuracy, Quadratic Weighted Kappa, Mean Absolute Error, and Pearson's correlation. We further conducted ablation studies to examine the contributions of reference interpretations and analytic rubrics to model performance, and initially explored whether interpreting direction affects model scoring behavior. title: Generative AI as a Learning Companion for Self‐Directed Second Language Learning Among Secondary School Students: A Mixed‐Methods Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Self‐directed Learning (SDL) is an important skill for learners of all ages and phases of life. Generative AI facilitates self‐directed second language (L2) learning by providing interactive, personalised access to online resources. However, existing research on AI‐assisted self‐directed L2 learning focuses on adult learners in higher education, leaving a gap in understanding how adolescent learners engage in SDL in secondary schools. This study addresses this gap by examining how secondary students engage with ChatGPT in self‐directed L2 learning and the extent to which they view it as a useful learning companion. Drawing on SDL theory and Candy's (1991) autodidaxy framework, we examined students' attitudes, behaviours, readiness, frequency of usage, and perceptions of ChatGPT's role in self‐directed L2 learning. Using a mixed‐methods approach, data were collected through a survey of 278 students and interviews with 15 participants. title: Multilingual Refugee Pre‐Service English Teachers Negotiating Their Professional Identity Through Translanguaging
abstract: ABSTRACT Although research on teacher identity has expanded significantly in today's globalizing world, the lived experiences of refugee teachers within broader discussions of multilingualism, identity, and educational policy are underexamined. Addressing this gap, the present study explores how multilingual refugee pre‐service English language teachers in Türkiye construct and negotiate their professional identities. Grounded in translanguaging theory, trauma‐informed pedagogy, and raciolinguistic ideologies, the study adopts a narrative inquiry design within a multiple‐case framework. Data were generated through interviews, narratives, field notes and analyzed thematically. The findings reveal that refugee pre‐service English language teachers employed four interconnected translanguaging orientations, i.e., compartmentalized, relational, transitional, and affective translanguaging, to negotiate identity. Furthermore, participants transformed experiences of translanguaging identity dissonance into forms of agentive linguistic repositioning. Implications are discussed.

title: Self‐Feedback and Self‐Assessment in Second Language Writing: A Critical Scoping Review and Future Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT Self‐assessment (SA) and self‐feedback (SF) have gained increasing attention in second language writing (L2) research as key mechanisms supporting self‐regulated learning and learner autonomy. However, as warned by some scholars, conceptual and methodological challenges still remain in understanding and exploring the two constructs in L2 writing research. This paper presents a critical scoping review of 33 studies on SA and SF in L2 writing to examine how these constructs have been conceptualized and studied, with the aim of identifying key theoretical and methodological challenges in the field. title: Recognising L2 Pragmatics Learning as a Morally Embedded and Psychologically Challenging Process
abstract: ABSTRACT Traditional understandings of pragmatic competence within the field of second language acquisition have tended to emphasise the learner's ability to successfully comprehend the pragmatic norms of ‘native speakers’ in terms of mappings between linguistic forms, functions, and context. Yet such theoretical understandings have tended not to acknowledge that engaging with new norms relating to common pragmatic acts such as greetings, requests, apologies, compliments, offers etc. is a morally embedded process that has the potential to challenge learners’ deep assumptions about socially (in)appropriate linguistic behaviour and generate negative evaluations of difference based on a sense of psychological threat. What this means is that models of pragmatic competence have not considered the need for learners to become able to manage the emotional tensions that emerge as part of their engagement with new linguistic practices and their attempts to establish a sense of legitimacy as social actors within the new language. title: From Learner‐Output Profiles to Textbook Input: Localizing Grammar Descriptors Through a Taiwanese K–12 Textbook Corpus
abstract: ABSTRACT External grammar profiles, such as the English Grammar Profile (EGP), provide Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR)‐linked descriptions of learner output, but their level assignments cannot be assumed to offer a ready‐made sequence for local instruction. What remains underexamined is how learner‐output‐based descriptors correspond to the grammatical input, non‐attestation, and sequencing patterns represented in school textbooks. This study addresses this gap by using Taiwan's government‐approved K–12 EFL textbooks as evidence of textbook‐based instructional input for examining the curriculum‐facing applicability of A1–B2 CEFR/EGP‐linked grammar descriptors. The analysis traced descriptor instantiation and non‐attestation, distributional salience across school stages, level mismatches between EGP benchmark placement and textbook sequencing, and rule‐based consolidation for pedagogical coherence. title: Positioning GenAI in Academic Research Discourse: Layered Grammatical Patterns and the Limits of a Single Agency Gradient
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is grammatically positioned in Discussion sections of GenAI‐related academic writing research. From 134 eligible articles, 50 were selected through year‐by‐topic stratified probability sampling, yielding 969 AI‐related occurrences and 1026 grammatical relations. We analysed three layers: rank, clause function, and Subject status. Valence was unrelated to the nominal–clausal boundary and to Participant–Circumstance status, but was associated with Clause versus Embedded_clause positioning; this association remained in paper‐robust and within‐paper analyses. Positive and Negative claims did not differ reliably in Subject status. Concordance analysis showed that embedded AI relations could occur within propositions asserted in ranking clauses. The findings show that grammatical dimensions of AI positioning pattern differently across evaluative contexts and should not be collapsed into a single agency gradient.

title: A Latent Profile Analysis of Chinese EFL Students’ Speaking Self‐Efficacy: The Role of Gender in Predicting Profile Membership and the Association of Profiles With Speaking Proficiency
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding learners’ English speaking self‐efficacy is essential for promoting effective oral communication in EFL contexts. However, variable‐centered research on English speaking self‐efficacy often overlooks heterogeneity among learners. Studies have reported mixed findings on the relationship between English speaking self‐efficacy and speaking proficiency, and the influence of gender remains unclear. To better capture learner variability and clarify these inconsistencies, this study adopted a person‐centered approach using latent profile analysis (LPA) to explore learner speaking self‐efficacy. It aimed to identify distinct self‐efficacy profiles, examine the role of gender in predicting profile membership, and assess the relationship between self‐efficacy and proficiency across profiles with data from 1410 students across four universities in China using a five‐dimensional English speaking self‐efficacy scale. title: Disrupting Dominant Ideologies in Chilean Teacher Education Through Ideological Clarity
abstract: ABSTRACT This study seeks to develop a more nuanced understanding of how English language teacher educators navigate the tensions between and across institutional expectations, the Chilean sociopolitical landscape, the increasing diversity and their pedagogical choices as they construct their professional identities. By examining how these educators negotiate and resist the hegemonic discourses and practices embedded and embodied in language teacher education, such as the valorisation of native‐speakerism, the devaluation of local knowledges, and the erasure of multilingual realities, this study highlights the centrality of cultivating linguistic ideological clarity. Such clarity is essential for challenging entrenched power structures and reimagining more equitable, inclusive, and contextually responsive language education. title: Situating Genre in Task‐Informed Second Language Writing Research
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper, a review of task‐informed second language writing research examining the effect(s) of various genres—in particular argumentative genres—on the linguistic complexity of written L2 performance, traces the treatment of genre in such studies. The review concludes that, from its early explanations of the cognitive complexity of argumentative genres to later explanations of the functional demands of argumentative genres, task‐informed L2 writing research often assumes the complexity of such genres but it crucially overlooks genre familiarity among participants. The analysis leads to some methodological recommendations which include a tripartite approach to examining the effect(s) of genre on the linguistic complexity of L2 written production.

title: Enhancing a Pre‐Service L2 Chinese Teacher's Knowledge and Skills in Teaching Pragmatics Through a Professional Development Course
abstract: ABSTRACT This study reports a case study on the development of a pre‐service second language (L2) Chinese teacher's knowledge and skills in teaching pragmatics through a 15‐week professional development (PD) course. From a sociocultural perspective, the course was designed to (a) provide the teacher with extensive exposure to academic concepts in pragmatics and instructional pragmatics, (b) engage her in languaging tasks that verbalized her conceptual understanding and fostered conscious reflection, and (c) offer opportunities for her to practically apply her conceptual knowledge. At the beginning and end of the course, the teacher completed questionnaires assessing her knowledge of pragmatics, along with her confidence and ability to teach it. Throughout the course, she participated in five monologic languaging tasks that articulated her conscious understanding of the concepts encountered during training. Toward the end of the course, the teacher had the opportunity to practically apply her conceptual knowledge by creating and presenting a lesson plan. title: Workplace Immersion and Intercultural Learning: Indonesian Japanese Language Learners in Internship Programs in Japan
abstract: ABSTRACT This study explores cross‐cultural immersion in a workplace environment among Japanese as L2 of Indonesian learners who participate in internship programs in Japan. Internship programs are often assumed to improve intercultural competence; little is understood about how such development is shaped through everyday workplace interaction. This study investigates how participants navigate language use, social expectation and cultural standard in situated work contexts. We use qualitative data from 29 participants, including in‐depth interviews and participant observations. The data are analyzed by the Critical Elements of Immersion Experience framework, with a focus on participants’ interactional workplace experience. title: Beyond Access: A Systematic Review of Turkish Language Education for Migrant Learners in Türkiye
abstract: ABSTRACT Focusing on Turkish as a second language (L2) education among migrant learners in Türkiye, this systematic review examines how empirical research has conceptualized the pedagogical, institutional, affective, and social conditions shaping Turkish language education between 2014 and 2025. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 72 peer‐reviewed empirical studies identified through TRDizin, ERIC, Scopus, and Web of Science were selected and analyzed. The studies were systematically coded for study characteristics and thematic dimensions. The findings indicate that Turkish language learning is not merely an individual process, but a relational, context‐dependent process shaped by pedagogical practices, teacher agency, social ecology, institutional conditions, and access to linguistic capital. The review identifies a segregation paradox whereby structural inclusion through school enrolment or integration classes does not necessarily foster meaningful interaction with host‐community peers. title: Negotiating Classroom Language Practices: Pre‐Service Teacher Agency and L1/L2 Decision‐Making in Exam‐Oriented EFL Classrooms
abstract: ABSTRACT Although multilingual perspectives have challenged English‐only norms, limited research has examined how pre‐service teachers translate contextual demands into L1/L2 decisions during practicum. This qualitative multiple‐case study involved 24 pre‐service English teachers during a 12‐week practicum in examination‐oriented Chinese senior high schools. Four focal participants underwent longitudinal within‐ and cross‐case analysis, while data from the remaining 20 were used to examine recurrence across the cohort. Data included observations, recordings, journals, interviews, and teaching artefacts. Three recurrent patterns emerged: lesson‐type‐based allocation, diagnostic switching, and L1‐supported meaning‐making towards L2 output. A less frequent extension involved coordinating multimodal and dialectal resources. title: Interaction‐Seeking Behavior in Second Language Learning: The Role of Regulatory Modes
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigated how trait‐level regulatory modes influenced L2 learners’ interaction‐seeking behavior (ISB) and L2 regulatory modes. To this end, 218 university‐level foreign language learners in the United States completed a questionnaire that measured their ISB and both general and L2‐specific regulatory modes. Factor analysis confirmed the two‐factor structure of ISB: Proactive interaction , concerned with seeking and engaging in interaction, and interaction monitoring , characterized by observing, evaluating, and adjusting one's L2 interaction behavior. Generalized additive models revealed that locomotion, a dispositional tendency to move from one state to another, predicted learners’ proactive interaction and interaction monitoring, whereas assessment, a dispositional tendency to think, evaluate, and analyze before acting, showed a more limited predictive role. title: English as a Lingua Franca‐Mediated Meaning‐Making and Intercultural Competence in TikTok Live–Based Language Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT As digitally mediated communication increasingly shapes language learning beyond formal classrooms, social media platforms offer new possibilities for authentic, intercultural interaction. This qualitative study investigates how TikTok Live‐mediated interaction supports English as a lingua franca (ELF) use, meaning‐making, and intercultural learning through collaborative and scaffolded practices. Grounded in Vygotskian sociocultural theory and research on scaffolding, the study conceptualizes TikTok Live as a socially mediated learning environment in which interaction, participation, and collaborative support shape language learning experiences. Data were generated from live‐streamed sessions and semi‐structured interviews with five English language teachers and fifteen adult learners across Indonesia, the Philippines, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam. Content analysis focused on ELF use, collaborative task engagement, inquiry‐driven interaction, and teacher and peer scaffolding. title: Comparing Human‐Created and NotebookLM‐Generated Podcasts for EAP Instruction: Differences in Linguistic Complexity and the Role of Prompt Design
abstract: ABSTRACT Science popularization podcasts are valuable resources for EAP instruction because they make academic content more accessible to learners. However, producing high‐quality podcasts is time‐consuming and resource‐intensive, and existing resources may not always align with instructional goals or learners’ needs. NotebookLM, a large language model (LLM)‐based tool, may offer possibilities for generating multimedia materials more efficiently. Yet, little is known about how linguistically comparable such AI‐generated podcasts are to human‐created ones or how prompt design may shape their linguistic complexity for pedagogical use. To address this gap, this study examined the lexical and syntactic complexity of human‐created and NotebookLM‐generated podcasts derived from the same research‐article source texts. Four corpora were analyzed: a corpus of human‐created podcasts from the Nature Podcast series and three corpora of NotebookLM‐generated podcasts produced under different conditions: the default setting (no prompt) and prompts intended to approximate CEFR B1‐ and B2‐level output for EAP instruction. title: Foreign Language Grit, Control‐Value Appraisals, and Writing Emotions Among Spanish L3 Learners: A Mediation and Network Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Writing emotions critically influence foreign language (FL) acquisition, yet existing research predominantly focuses on the anxiety‐enjoyment dichotomy in English learning contexts, overlooking boredom as a key negative emotion and multilingual learners (e.g., Spanish L3). Concurrently, while FL grit emerges as a pivotal trait for emotional regulation, its interplay with control‐value theory (CVT) in shaping enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom remains empirically unexamined. This study examines the relationship between FL grit and writing emotions (enjoyment, anxiety, boredom) among Spanish L3 learners, drawing on CVT. Bootstrap mediation analysis and psychological network analysis of data from 152 Chinese college Spanish L3 learners revealed that FL grit is directly and positively related to writing enjoyment, while negatively with writing anxiety and writing boredom. title: These Are Not My Words: Writer‐AI Alignment, Template Attraction, and Verification in AI‐Mediated EFL Writing at a Jordanian Public University
abstract: ABSTRACT Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is now widely used in L2 writing, but much existing research still relies on learner attitudes rather than traceable evidence of writing behaviour. This study examines how Jordanian EFL writers judged, used, revised, verified, and sometimes rejected AI‐generated language during actual composing. It asks how students evaluated the alignment between AI wording and their intended meaning, voice, genre purpose, and evidential responsibility; what uptake pathways they followed when working with AI output; and how verification shaped revision depth and authorial ownership. The study draws on a qualitative‐led multiple‐case design with embedded descriptive episode analysis. Thirty second‐year English majors at a Jordanian public university completed three course‐based assignments: a personal narrative, a source‐based argument essay, and a public‐facing opinion piece. title: Exploring the Effects of Genre on Digital Multimodal Composing Performance in Chinese as a Second Language (CSL): A Cross‐Genre Analysis of Linguistic Features and Multimodal Resource Design
abstract: ABSTRACT Although digital multimodal composing (DMC) has been widely implemented across genres in second‐language (L2) instruction, genre‐based differences in learners’ DMC performance remain underexplored. Existing research has primarily focused on linguistic features, with limited attention to genre's influence on multimodal resource design. This study involved nine learners of Chinese as a second language (CSL), who completed narrative, expository, and argumentative DMC tasks. A total of 27 DMC compositions were collected and analyzed quantitatively and qualitatively in terms of two dimensions—linguistic features and multimodal resource design—to examine the effect of genre on CSL learners’ DMC performance. The results revealed significant genre‐based differences in fluency, error‐free T‐unit rate, T‐unit syntactic error rate, lexical sophistication (Levels 1 and 3), and syntactic complexity. title: How Is L2 Grit Positioned in Chinese College EFL Learners’ Network of Anxiety, Boredom, and Psychological Need Frustration? A Psychological Network Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how domain‐specific L2 grit is conditionally associated with foreign language anxiety, foreign language boredom, and basic psychological need frustration among Chinese university EFL learners. Drawing on Complex Dynamic Systems Theory as a systems‐oriented heuristic, we use psychological network analysis to model these variables as an interconnected set of contemporaneous associations. Survey data were collected from 908 university students enrolled in English courses. Participants completed established scales measuring L2 grit, foreign language anxiety, classroom boredom, and psychological need frustration. To capture the interrelations among these constructs, we estimated a Gaussian graphical model in which factor scores derived from CFA‐estimated latent constructs were represented as nodes and regularized partial correlations were represented as edges. title: Off‐Task Talk to Manage Relationship Work During Student Group Work in Second Language Classrooms
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper presents a conversation analytic study on student relationship work in off‐task talk (OTT) during group work in foreign language classrooms. Often seen as disengagement from tasks, OTT's social and relational functions in student classroom group interaction and formation remain underexplored. This study provides a local interactional account of how OTT creates a social and interactional space for students to navigate emergent group memberships during their language learning. Video and audio recordings of student group interactions in senior high school English classrooms in China were collected, transcribed and analysed. The data captures instances where students share personal experiences, feelings and perspectives unrelated to tasks mostly using their first language. OTT is observed to emerge from on‐task talk and contextual classroom elements. The data also shows that self‐disclosures prompt reciprocal sharing during OTT. title: Motivational Reorganization in Online Chinese Learning: A Longitudinal Q Methodology Study of Greek Beginner Learners
abstract: ABSTRACT With the expansion of digital education, online Chinese language teaching has grown worldwide, yet learners’ motivational development in European contexts remains underexplored. Grounded in Complex Dynamic Systems Theory and the L2 Motivational Self System, this study employed longitudinal Q methodology to investigate motivational reorganization among 15 Greek beginner learners in a 16‐week online Chinese course. Data were collected through Q sorting at Weeks 2 and 16, supplemented by post‐sorting and retrospective interviews. The analysis identified three dominant motivational trajectories: Vague to Culture‐anchored, Vague to Disengagement, and Career‐anchored instrumental to Instrument–culture integrated, alongside two cross‐dimensional transition cases. Findings show that Sino‐Hellenic resonance emerged as an important contextual source of motivational meaning, encompassing both cultural‐historical affinities and contemporary economic and professional connections. title: Motivational Variability of Second Language Learning and Self‐Regulation: A Comparison Between Profiles in South Korea
abstract: ABSTRACT Motivation plays a pivotal role in second/foreign language (L2) learning, yet it often fluctuates in response to academic and emotional challenges. Despite its importance, the temporal variability of L2 learning motivation remains underexplored. To address this gap, the present study examined the motivational trajectories of 33 Korean university students majoring in English education, with a focus on how self‐regulation strategies interact with motivational variability. Motivational trajectories were retrospectively reconstructed based on self‐rated motigraphs collected at a single time point, together with written reflections analyzing learning experiences across school years, with particular attention to four key participants. Based on motivation patterns and a scatter plot of average motivation and standard deviation, participants were categorized into two contrastive focal profiles: High Motivation, Low Variability (HMLV) and Low Motivation, High Variability (LMHV). title: Investigating the Predictive Power of Grammatical Metaphor Nominalization as Lexical Complexity Benchmarks for EFL Writing Quality
abstract: ABSTRACT Grammatical metaphor (GM) has been empirically demonstrated to have a significant positive correlation with the quality of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing, with higher‐scoring writings tending to utilize a greater number of GMs. Among the various types of GM, grammatical metaphor nominalization (GMN) is a key focus when examining EFL writing. The GMN use is commonly measured by its normalized frequency within a text or GMN density, an index that falls within the dimension of lexical complexity and considers the overall presence of GMN. However, it is essential to separately analyze the frequencies of GMN subtypes, such as Process as Thing realized by deverbal nouns and Quality as Thing realized by deadjectival nouns. Furthermore, when evaluating the EFL writing quality, it is crucial to explore additional dimensions of GMN complexity, including the GMN sophistication and GMN diversity. title: Understanding Learner Beliefs With Complexity Theory: Insights From Academic Presentation
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the recognized importance of learner beliefs in second and foreign language learning, research specifically exploring EFL learner beliefs about academic presentations remains limited. Moreover, few studies have approached learner beliefs as a complex system. Drawing on complexity theory, this study employed a multiple‐case study design involving six EFL learners in EAP settings. Data were triangulated from classroom observations, semi‐structured interviews, stimulated recalls, presentation slides, and self‐reflection documents. The findings conceptualize learner beliefs and practices as an integrated complex system (i.e., belief‐practice system). abstract: ABSTRACT Alignment is the key mechanism through which the continuation task promotes language acquisition, yet the effect of input text complexity on alignment has been examined only through binary simplified‐versus‐unsimplified comparisons, leaving it unclear how the relationship is shaped and whether different alignment layers respond differently. The present study established three complexity levels (low, medium, high) and measured alignment at three levels—lexical (LRR, LSS), phrasal (4‐gram borrowing), and syntactic (relative clauses, participial adverbials). Eighty‐seven Chinese university students who had passed the College English Test Band 4 (CET‐4) completed continuation tasks for three narrative texts in a within‐subjects repeated‐measures design; data were analyzed using repeated‐measures ANOVA/ANCOVA with comprehension as a covariate, generalized linear mixed‐effects models for low‐base‐rate syntactic indices, and orthogonal polynomial contrasts to test for non‐linearity. title: “There's Pressure to Use Standard English”: Lingering Linguicism in the Work of Signed Language Interpreters
abstract: ABSTRACT Applied linguistics and interpreting have much in common; however, the education of signed language interpreters in the States provides barely any applied linguistics training. Linguistic racism (linguicism) frames the education and evaluation of sign language interpreters. Mainstream English is consciously and subconsciously valued by practitioners. This research is the first in the field by exploring the biases working practitioners possess about African American Vernacular English (AAVE). Twenty interpreters were interviewed, and 100% reported that standard English is of primary importance when working. Seventeen indicated that they can understand the majority of spoken AAVE. To test this, they listened to and then retold a 1 min 10 s AAVE narrative. When retelling, they omitted 53% of the narrative AAVE content, achieving just a 47% mean accuracy score.

title: Exploring the Impact of Anxiety on Chinese‐English Consecutive Interpreting: Cognitive Trade‐Off Patterns
abstract: ABSTRACT Interpreting is a cognitively demanding activity that can elicit heightened anxiety, particularly among student interpreters. Although prior research has linked anxiety to performance deficits, little is known about its differential effects across linguistic dimensions and the potential cognitive trade‐offs under varying task conditions. This study, employing a mixed‐methods design, examines the impact of anxiety on Chinese‐English consecutive interpreting, focusing on lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, and speech disfluency and examining the moderating role of topic familiarity. Forty‐two graduate students in Translation and Interpreting Program completed two consecutive interpreting tasks differing in topic familiarity, followed by assessments using Interpreting Anxiety Scale and NASA‐TLX cognitive load measurement and semi‐structured interviews. Linear mixed‐effects models revealed that anxiety significantly increased speech disfluency, with topic familiarity moderating this effect. In contrast, lexical diversity and syntactic complexity remained largely stable, except for selective interactions with cognitive load. Qualitative analysis corroborated these findings

title: Feedback Configurations in Interpreting Teaching: Understanding Teachers’ Feedback Belief‐Practice Tensions
abstract: ABSTRACT Teachers’ beliefs are noted not to always align with their practices, and such mismatches may in fact reflect teachers’ situated responses to contextual demands. Existing studies have largely focused on corrective feedback in second language teaching and typically examined feedback dimensions in isolation, restraining understanding of how multiple dimensions co‐occur in authentic classroom interaction and relate to teachers’ belief‐practice tensions. Given the inherently multidimensional nature of interpreting teaching, this study examined nine undergraduate interpreting teachers’ feedback beliefs and practices. Drawing on classroom observations, semi‐structured interviews, correlation analysis, and hierarchical cluster analysis, the study identified two major tensions concerning feedback explicitness (implicit vs. explicit) and recipients (individual vs. group). Three recurring feedback configurations emerged: performance‐oriented critical feedback, specific supportive feedback, and general praise‐oriented feedback. title: Emotions and Sensemaking in EMI Teaching: An Autoethnography of a Vietnamese Lecturer in Taiwan
abstract: ABSTRACT This autoethnography explores how I, a novice Vietnamese lecturer in Taiwan, made sense of and responded to emotional tensions in an English‐medium instruction (EMI) classroom. Drawing on personal journals and teaching notes from September 2025 to January 2026, it focuses on four tensions: students’ language use, classroom silence, dependence on oral explanation, and care versus consistency in assessment. Teacher sensemaking guided analysis of how ambiguous cues were noticed, interpreted, reconsidered, and translated into pedagogical action. Initial interpretations often linked communication difficulties to personal inadequacy, but reflection led to more cautious, provisional understandings. Detailed slides, written instructions, reminders, and individualized feedback expanded access to course information while increasing instructional labor. In assessment, care was reinterpreted as transparency and consistent application of shared criteria. The study highlights the linguistic and professional in‐betweenness of an international EMI lecturer and the need for preparation in multilingual interaction, pedagogical responsibility, emotional vulnerability, and instructional labor

title: Proficiency Without Interaction: Comparing Stance and Engagement in LLM‐Generated and Human CEFR Writing
abstract: ABSTRACT This study compared the linguistic resources writers use to express attitudes, signal certainty, and interact with readers, that is, stance and engagement patterns. We examined these patterns in large language model (LLM)‐generated essays and human learner essays across Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) levels A2 through C1. title: Unveiling Bidirectional Relationships Between Foreign Language Enjoyment and Growth Language Mindset: A Longitudinal Study
abstract: ABSTRACT This longitudinal study examined the bidirectional relationships between growth language mindset (GLM) and foreign language enjoyment (FLE) at both the construct and subdimension levels. Questionnaire data were collected from 550 Chinese university EFL learners across three waves in one semester. The cross‐lagged panel model (CLPM) was employed to examine the bidirectional relationship between GLM and FLE, and cross‐lagged panel networks were estimated to capture subdimension‐specific longitudinal associations. At the construct level, bidirectional relationships were found between GLM and FLE across both intervals, with the GLM→FLE path significantly stronger in the later interval. At the subdimension level, the primary networks identified a broader pattern of cross‐construct lagged associations, retaining nine pathways from Wave 1 to Wave 2 and 14 from Wave 2 to Wave 3. title: Mental Simulation in Color‐Implied Sentence Comprehension Differs Across Languages for Late Chinese‐English Bilinguals
abstract: ABSTRACT The present study examined whether late Chinese‐English bilinguals engage in color‐based mental simulation during first‐language (L1 Chinese) and second‐language (L2 English) sentence comprehension and whether such simulation is modulated by object color typicality. Participants completed a sentence‐picture verification (SPV) task in both Chinese and English using objects with typical and atypical colors. Results revealed a more robust color‐match effect in L1 Chinese than in L2 English, indicating stronger color‐based mental simulation during L1 sentence comprehension. Across languages, participants responded faster to typically colored objects than to atypically colored objects, demonstrating an overall facilitative effect of object color typicality on reaction time. Moreover, object color typicality influenced the color‐match effect differently across languages. In L1 Chinese, significant color‐match effects were observed for both typical and atypical objects, whereas in L2 English, a significant color‐match effect was observed only for atypical objects. title: Growing Like Ivy: Exploring EFL Teachers’ Transformative Agency in the GenAI Context Based on the Double Stimulation Principle
abstract: ABSTRACT The double stimulation principle explains how individuals resolve conflicts by introducing auxiliary stimuli to solve problems. Drawing on this principle, this study investigated how three English‐as‐a‐foreign‐language (EFL) teachers developed transformative agency through the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools into teaching. The study was conducted in a junior high school that had organised a four‐day GenAI training programme for its teachers. Data were collected through interviews, classroom observations, and authentic teaching materials that reflected the teachers’ practices. The findings indicated that the teachers who had the same training experience adopted diverse GenAI‐integrated teaching practices and developed transformative agency along divergent trajectories, analogous to ivy branches growing in different directions from a common root. The training requirements served as the first stimulus, triggering motivational conflicts between the teachers’ concerns regarding the quality of GenAI output and their desire to enhance work efficiency. title: Translanguaging Trails: Tracing a Multilingual Writer's Repertoire‐in‐Motion Across Digital Platforms
abstract: ABSTRACT Multilingual writers increasingly build meaning across digital platforms, yet translanguaging research has largely observed one space, on one platform, at a time. How meaning travels between those sites, and what that movement makes possible, remains difficult to see. A multilingual speaker in Melbourne sets out to translate collective storytelling into Chinese, Korean, and Japanese for an academic presentation. Over two weeks, she works across Word documents, KakaoTalk, email, and WhatsApp, drawing on her character‐based literacy and three language networks. A Chinese semantic distinction shapes how she reads her Korean options, and a Korean concept seeds her Japanese formulation, so the translation she settles on takes shape across all four platforms. We offer translanguaging trails as a way of seeing this: the path a writer's repertoire takes across tools, languages, and interlocutors over time, the line that connects otherwise separate sites and becomes visible only across them. title: Performance Control, Reflection, and Attainment in Instructed Language Learning: A Longitudinal Study of Self‐Regulation in L2 English and L2 German Courses
abstract: ABSTRACT Self‐regulation (SR) plays a central role in instructed language learning, as it enables learners to set goals, monitor progress, and adapt learning behaviour through reflection. We investigate the contribution of two core self‐regulatory processes—performance control (PC) and reflection (R)—to attainment (A) in structure‐focused L2 English and L2 German courses. In the context of our study, these courses are taught to language majors and involve explicit, analytically oriented instruction in language structure, including phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics, rather than skills‐focused language teaching. Addressing calls to move beyond self‐report measures, we drew on behavioural indicators of self‐regulation, including engagement in non‐graded Moodle activities and participation in structured reflection tasks. Data was collected longitudinally at four time points over one academic year from 119 learners enrolled in English L2/German L3 ( n = 70) and German L2/English L3 ( n = 49) programmes. title: Configurating Learner Engagement in AI‐Mediated Informal Digital Learning of English: A Combined Serial Mediation and FsQCA Approach
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the growing prevalence of AI‐mediated informal digital learning of English (AI‐IDLE), the complex configuration of cognitive‐affective factors underpinning learner engagement remains inadequately understood. Grounded in control‐value theory (CVT), this study employed a dual‐analytical approach—integrating structural equation modeling (SEM) and fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA)—to examine learner engagement in AI‐IDLE among 796 Chinese EFL learners. The results demonstrated (1) AI‐IDLE exerts a significant direct predictive effect on learner engagement. title: Real‐Time Changes in Enjoyment, Boredom, and Engagement in English Classes: Evidence From Polish Learners and Teachers
abstract: ABSTRACT Although research has increasingly examined individual differences in second language acquisition, less attention has been paid to how specific emotions and engagement change during secondary‐school lessons. This study examined within‐lesson variation in enjoyment, boredom, and engagement, the associations of enjoyment and boredom with engagement, and differences between student and teacher ratings. Participants were 244 Polish students from 19 intact classes and their 19 teachers, with data collected during one English lesson in each class. Students rated enjoyment, boredom, and engagement on a five‐point scale across four 10‐min segments and completed short post‐lesson reports. Teachers provided parallel class‐level ratings and reports. Quantitative data were analyzed using regression models with student‐clustered robust standard errors, time‐period and lesson fixed effects, and a time‐period × lesson interaction where appropriate. title: Navigating Ideological Tensions: Pre‐Service Teachers’ Beliefs and Practices of Translanguaging in ESL Classrooms
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how pre‐service teachers (PSTs) in Hong Kong developed beliefs about translanguaging and how they enacted and negotiated these beliefs during teaching practicums in English‐as‐a‐second‐language (ESL) classrooms. Drawing on reflective diaries and follow‐up interviews with nine PSTs, the study found that PSTs’ beliefs were shaped through ongoing negotiations among competing discourses encountered in teacher education programmes and practicum experiences. Although participants frequently drew on multilingual, multimodal, and semiotic resources to support comprehension and participation, their practices were largely oriented towards pragmatic instructional goals rather than the broader transformative aims associated with translanguaging pedagogy. Importantly, this discrepancy reflected not simply a failure of implementation but the ways in which PSTs exercised agency while navigating institutional constraints and contextual realities. title: Academic English Literacy as a Moderator of the Relationship Between Psychological Capital and Academic Success in English Medium Instruction
abstract: ABSTRACT In English Medium Instruction (EMI) contexts, students face simultaneous linguistic and academic demands. Although psychological capital (PsyCap) has been recognized as an important psychological resource for academic success, less is known about whether its effects depend on students’ academic English literacy (AEL). This study examined the associations between PsyCap dimensions and academic success, and whether these associations varied with students’ AEL in EMI settings. Structural equation modeling showed that hope ( β = 0.16), self‐efficacy ( β = 0.19), and resilience ( β = 0.20) were positively associated with academic success, whereas optimism was not ( β = 0.01). Moderation analyses further indicated that the positive associations of self‐efficacy and resilience with academic success were stronger at higher levels of AEL, while interactions involving hope and optimism were not statistically significant. The findings highlight the dimension‐specific and conditional nature of PsyCap in EMI contexts and underscore the role of AEL as a key enabling factor linking psychological resources to academic success.

title: From Symbolic Success to Meaningful Use: Distinct Effects of Syntax‐Focused and Meaning‐Focused AI‐Assisted English Learning on Performative and Affective Factors
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examined the distinct effects of syntax‐focused and meaning‐focused AI‐assisted English learning on learners’ performative and affective outcomes. Drawing on Searle's Chinese Room hypothesis, the study distinguished formal accuracy from meaningful language use to examine whether AI‐supported learning produced uniform or differentiated development. A quasi‐experimental pretest‐posttest design was conducted with 160 non‐English‐major university students assigned to either a syntax‐focused or meaning‐focused condition. Analyses of covariance and mediation models were applied while controlling for prior language mastery and digital literacy. The results showed that AI‐assisted English learning was effective, but its effects differed by instructional orientation. The syntax‐focused condition led to significantly higher syntactic performance, whereas the meaning‐focused condition produced higher meaning‐level performance, social presence, and willingness to communicate. Social presence showed statistically significant indirect associations between learning condition and both meaning‐level performance and willingness to communicate, but not syntactic performance. title: Reimagining Task‐Based Language Teaching: An Intervention Study With Young Novice Learners
abstract: ABSTRACT In the field of second language acquisition, the growing emphasis on fostering communicative competence has brought task‐based language learning (TBLT) into the spotlight. Yet, empirical studies on TBLT with young novice learners in foreign language settings are notably lacking due to several factors associated with the cognitive and social‐emotional characteristics of young novice learners. To address these challenges, the cognitive sustainability framework was proposed; TBLT for this population of learners should be structured as a sequence of interconnected tasks culminating in a personally relevant end‐product, requiring multiple sessions to complete. This approach allows for systematic integration of progressively complex targeted vocabulary and syntax. Empirical validation of this framework was undertaken through a quasi‐experimental intervention study involving young novice Korean‐speaking learners of English. Results from repeated multivariate analyses of variance provide substantial support for the cognitive sustainability theory and shed light on crucial elements of TBLT overlooked in previous research.

title: Dreaming and Living the Globalized World Through IELTS: A Case Study of Bangladeshi Test‐Takers
abstract: ABSTRACT This case study investigated the lived experiences of 10 IELTS test‐takers from Bangladesh. It explored their motivations for taking the test as well as their test experiences during and after the test. It demonstrates how the participants sought to position themselves in the imagined community through renegotiating their identities to climb up the ladder of success through higher studies by taking IELTS. However, not all participants’ dreams to live in a globalized world could come true either due to visa rejection or refusal of admission from universities. The study also reveals challenges that these test‐takers faced during the test because it was unrelated to their education system, raising questions around whether tests can be distanced from test‐takers’ lives and realities. This study argues for a global test that not only measures English proficiency authentically but also aligns with the education system that test‐takers are familiar with.

title: Linguistic Distance and Syntactic Complexity in L2 Writing: A Dependency‐Based Analysis Across 17 L1 Backgrounds
abstract: ABSTRACT Syntactic complexity is a central dimension of second language (L2) writing proficiency, yet it remains underexplored how it varies across learners from diverse first‐language (L1) backgrounds and whether such variation can be explained by linguistic distance. Drawing on a corpus of English writing produced by L2 learners from 17 L1 backgrounds, this study examines the effect of L1 background on syntactic complexity using Mean Dependency Distance (MDD) and Mean Hierarchical Distance (MHD) and tests the explanatory power of linguistic distance. The results show that L1 background has a significant effect on syntactic complexity in L2 writing. MDD and MHD are positively correlated, suggesting an integrated property of syntactic organization. Cluster analysis identifies three relatively distinct groups among the 17 L1 backgrounds, indicating that patterns of syntactic complexity are better captured by data‐driven groupings than by traditional language classifications. title: Assessing EFL Learners’ Phraseological Competence Through Association Measures: The Role of Reference Corpus Selection
abstract: ABSTRACT Association measures, such as pointwise mutual information (PMI), have been widely used to explore learners’ phraseological competence. Yet, the validity of PMI‐based evaluations critically depends on the reference corpus employed, and the extent to which this methodological choice affects assessment outcomes has not been systematically examined. This study investigates how reference corpus selection influences PMI scores and, consequently, the evaluation of learners’ phraseological competence. title: Co‐Teaching in a Virtual Intensive Study Language Programme: Insights From Team Ethnography
abstract: ABSTRACT As virtual study abroad becomes an increasingly important form of international education, little is known about how transnational teaching is organised and sustained across institutions. Using activity theory as an analytical framework and team ethnography as methodology, this study examines a virtual intensive study (VIS) programme delivered through collaboration between home‐ and host‐country teachers during the COVID‐19 pandemic. The dataset consists of four lesson recordings, 10 student interviews, two teacher focus group interviews, 21 sets of field notes and programme artefacts. The findings show that VIS generated educational, personal and social benefits and enhanced student engagement, speaking confidence and intercultural awareness. The virtual format broadened access and inclusivity and created opportunities for meaningful language use. The study also identifies systematic tension across the activity system. title: Generative AI, Linguistic Hierarchies and Unequal Access in Under‐Resourced Educational Contexts
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite growing enthusiasm around generative AI (GenAI) as a transformative force in education, access to these technologies remains profoundly unequal. This qualitative study examines how educators and students in under‐resourced Chinese educational contexts experience unequal access to GenAI and interpret its consequences for language learning, teaching and local knowledge production. Informed by critical sociolinguistics and political economy, the study draws on ten semi‐structured interviews with six teachers/educators and four students from local universities, rural communities and linguistically minoritised settings in China. The analysis shows that GenAI access is rarely a binary matter of presence or absence, but a layered set of hurdles that participants had to navigate actively: tools are visible through media, training sessions and peer networks, but unstable connectivity, outdated devices, paywalls, institutional permissions and limited local integration meant that turning visibility into sustained use required ongoing effort, workaround strategies and situated forms of agency. title: The Cognate Facilitation Effect of L2–L3 Cognates in Chinese–English–Spanish Trilinguals: The Role of L2 Proficiency
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on the cognate facilitation effect (CFE) in sequential bilinguals and trilinguals' lexical processing has offered important insights into the structure of the multilingual mental lexicon. A key cross‐linguistic factor that has received particular attention is second language (L2) proficiency, yet its role in different‐script trilinguals remains underexplored. The present study addressed this issue in L2 and L3 lexical processing among Chinese–English–Spanish trilinguals using lexical decision tasks. By manipulating L2 proficiency and measuring the strength of CFE through reaction times and accuracy, the study aimed to investigate orthographic‐overlap‐driven, form‐based cross‐language activation between the two non‐native languages. The findings provide preliminary evidence that the strength of form‐based L2–L3 cross‐language activation may vary with L2 proficiency, and they are compatible with the possibility that more entrenched lexical representations reduce reliance on orthographic overlap during visual word recognition.

title: Typing Chinese: Using Keyboard to Relieve Learners’ Foreign Language Anxiety in Chinese Character Online Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT Foreign language anxiety (FLA) is an important emotional variable affecting language learning. However, previous research has mainly focused on listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills. Less attention is given to the Chinese character writing system and its emotional impact. This study investigates the effects of typing and handwriting on FLA and learning performance among zero‐proficiency Chinese learners from Myanmar in an online learning context. Adopting an explanatory sequential mixed‐methods design, the research analyzes differences between the two groups through questionnaires, tests, and interviews. The results indicate that the writing medium significantly influences both the level and function of anxiety. Typing generated higher levels of anxiety, and this anxiety was associated with increased concentration and learning engagement. In contrast, handwriting is associated with lower levels of anxiety. However, this anxiety is more likely to be debilitating, reducing learners’ confidence and performance. title: “Black and White” or “White and Black”: The Processing of L1–L2 Structurally/Semantically Congruent Binomials by Japanese Learners of English
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigated whether L1–L2 structural/semantic congruency affects the processing of binomials in L2 English. Specifically, it aimed to examine how L2 learners process form‐meaning congruent binomials (completely‐congruent), semantically congruent but incongruent in form (reverse‐congruent), and incongruent (L1‐ and L2‐only) binomials compared to a baseline. Using reaction time data from a phrase decision task with 124 Japanese learners of English and 80 L1 English speakers as a control, the results revealed that L2 learners exhibited a significant processing advantage for both completely‐congruent and reverse‐congruent binomials over the baseline. In contrast, incongruent binomials showed no significant processing advantage. Furthermore, while L1 English speakers were sensitive to L2 (English) phrase frequency, L2 learners' processing was more robustly influenced by L1 (Japanese) phrase frequency, with L2 frequency showing no significant effect. title: “It Can't be Translated Into a Conventional English Phrase” : Crafting Academic Identities Through Translingual Writing
abstract: ABSTRACT This qualitative multiple case study explores multilingual postgraduate students’ academic identities through writing at an EMI university in Hong Kong, with a focus on how they gain legitimacy in knowledge‑making with their multilingual repertoires. Grounded in a poststructuralist understanding of identities as fluid and negotiated, the study takes writing as a key site where such identities are continually shaped. Adopting a translingual view, it investigates writing as an emergent meaning‑making process and as the synergy of meaning‐making resources across languages, spaces, and roles. The study gathered data from interview narratives and written artefacts produced by two focal participants, which document their translingual writing practices and the emergence of more legitimate identities in their disciplinary communities. The findings reveal that multilinguals craft fluid identities by drawing on linguistic items, culturally embedded concepts, and locally situated values to revoice legitimate meaning‐making practice. title: Individual Differences and Task Complexity in Second Language Writing: A Methodological Review
abstract: ABSTRACT This article provides a methodological review of empirical studies on second language (L2) writing and task complexity that have investigated the role of learner individual differences (IDs) in L2 writing processes and outcomes. Thirty journal articles published between 2005 and 2025 were coded for key theoretical, methodological (including ID measurement and analytical practices), and contextual characteristics. We identified thirty researched IDs, with L2 proficiency, working memory capacity, and L2 writing anxiety emerging as the most commonly investigated. Expanding insights from previous methodological reviews in task‐based language teaching (TBLT) (e.g., Bryfonski et al. 2024; Plonsky and Kim, 2016), we pinpoint and discuss common practices in theoretical orientation, ID instrumentation, overall study design, task design and implementation, and coding and analysis, among others. We also provide methodological recommendations in various domains and highlight promising avenues for future research.

title: Metacognitive Instruction to Enhance EFL Writers’ Metacognition, Feedback Uptake, and Revision Performance in a GenAI‐Assisted Feedback Context
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigated the impact of a metacognitive instruction (MI) intervention on EFL writers’ metacognition, feedback uptake, and revision performance in a Generative AI (GenAI)‐assisted feedback environment. The MI intervention integrated prompt engineering into EFL writing pedagogy following a four‐step MI sequence. Participants were 141 EFL learners recruited from a Chinese university, with 71 allocated to the experimental group (EG), which received the MI intervention, and 70 assigned to the control group (CG), which engaged with GenAI feedback without additional scaffolding. Following a pretest–posttest quasi‐experimental design, data were collected from multiple sources, including questionnaires, reflective journals, think‐aloud protocols, and draft and revised writing products. Results showed that the MI intervention significantly improved students’ strategy knowledge and all dimensions of metacognitive strategy use. title: Racialized and Sexualized Branding in Japan's Online Eikaiwa Industry: The Objectification of Female Eastern European Teachers
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how an online eikaiwa (English conversation) provider in Japan that employs only female Eastern European (particularly Ukrainian) teachers brands them through objectification. Analysis of textual and visual elements of the provider's website and related media, including videos, demonstrates that the teachers are objectified as attractive, beautiful Eastern European women , which is reinforced by viewers’ comments on the videos. Such objectification shapes and is shaped by the discourse in Japanese society that associates Ukraine with beautiful women. Although these findings closely parallel those of research on the learner‐driven gendered construction of female Filipino teachers, this article foregrounds the provider's racialized and sexualized branding of female Eastern European teachers as a strategy to differentiate itself from competitors. Tracing Interconnected Development in Self‐Directed L2 Learning: Journal Writing as a Window Into L2 Change in a Longitudinal Case Study
abstract: ABSTRACT This exploratory longitudinal case study investigates the one‐year L2 English development of a working adult engaged in self‐directed learning, focusing on the activities, resources, and contexts that influenced the participant's progress. Drawing on longitudinal quantitative and qualitative data, journal entries and monthly essays were collected and analyzed, along with interviews, surveys, session notes, and email exchanges to explore the participant's perspectives on L2 learning and selected learning approaches and resources. This case illustrates the dynamic, non‐linear nature of the participant's L2 development, including the interconnected influence of learning resources, the emergence of syntactically complex structures, and shifts in perceptions of English in relation to diverse learning materials. These outcomes suggest that, in this case, L2 development emerged through interacting cognitive, affective, and contextual factors rather than linear cause–effect relationships. Given the single‐case design, the findings offer case‐based insights into the dynamic processes underlying self‐directed L2 learning.

title: Agency‐Structure Dynamics in the Linguistic Landscape of a Global Mega‐Event: The 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics
abstract: ABSTRACT This article advances an agency‐structure perspective on linguistic landscapes (LLs) by examining the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics as a global mega‐event held during the pandemic. Drawing on geosemiotic analysis of multilingual signs and displays, it conceptualizes the LL not only as a collection of texts but as a social and discursive space in which actors’ practices and institutional arrangements are mutually constitutive. The findings show how the Chinese government, as the primary organizer, macro‐designed the visual‐linguistic environment to comply with long‐standing Olympic conventions and address the need for COVID‐19 prevention measures, while projecting China's cultural confidence on the world stage. Meanwhile, participants, audiences and individuals exercised agency within the event's time‐space structures, inserting their own signs and messages into public view. title: Sustaining Translanguaging Pedagogies: Teacher‐Learners’ Approaches Toward L2 Motivational Development in the Thai EFL Context
abstract: ABSTRACT Although translanguaging research in applied linguistics has investigated the use of the first language and multilingualism in classroom‐based settings, few studies have illustrated how English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers enact and sustain translanguaging pedagogies in their second language (L2) teaching in the Thai EFL context. This paper reports on how four teacher‐learners (TLs) on an international teaching practicum integrated translanguaging into their teaching praxis while engaging in professional development to make sense of translanguaging pedagogies. Audio‐recorded dialogues between the authors and TLs were analyzed using interpretive phenomenological analysis. The analysis revealed how TLs’ teaching praxis (1) made sense of translanguaging, (2) negotiated pedagogical and relational boundaries of L1 use, and (3) built co‐learning spaces and engagement. Drawing on these findings, we argue sustained professional dialogue facilitates dialogic spaces where TLs can position and interrogate their teaching knowledge, linguistic identities, and accumulated learning and teaching experiences. title: Task Complexity Effects on Writing Processes and Correlations With Text Features
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on task complexity (TC) effects on second language (L2) text features is abundant and has contributed critical insights. Comparatively, less is known about how L2 writers respond cognitively to diverse TC conditions or about potential effects of such processing activity on the characteristics of the texts produced. To expand on previous research, this study examined (i) the effects of TC on L2 writers’ processing activity (operationalized as on‐line writing behaviors and macro writing processes) globally and across three time intervals; and (ii) any potential relationship of processing activity with text features (as measured by complexity, accuracy, and fluency indices). In an intra‐subject design study, 45 advanced L2 English users completed two argumentative writing tasks (in time‐compressed conditions) that varied in cognitive complexity, operationally defined as the provision of ±content support. Processing activity was captured with the keystroke logging software Inputlog, together with a self‐rating post‐task questionnaire. title: L2 Chinese Grammatical Acquisition and Processing: A Substantive and Methodological Review
abstract: ABSTRACT This study presents a systematic review of 92 empirical studies on Chinese as a second language (CSL) in grammatical processing and development, synthesizing their substantive foci and methodological characteristics. The results reveal consistent scholarly attention to cross‐linguistic topics, with less focus on features that are distinctively salient in Chinese. Methodologically, studies most commonly relied on quantitative approaches and judgment tasks, while the use of online measures emerged only after 2014. We also identified several persistent challenges, including an overreliance on English‐speaking university students as participants, inconsistent proficiency assessment practices across studies, and limitations in transparent data reporting. In light of these limitations, we call for the adoption of a broader range of methodological tools, the inclusion of more diverse participants, varied research designs, and statistical techniques to enhance the rigor of CSL research and its contribution to the broader SLA field.

title: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence to Support Secondary Students’ Cognitive Processes in Writing
abstract: ABSTRACT While the benefits of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in supporting various cognitive processes in writing have been documented, most research has examined single stages of the writing process and focused on university students. This study addresses this gap by developing a domain‐specific GenAI chatbot and embedding it within a process‐based writing instruction (PBWI) program to explore its effectiveness and challenges in supporting secondary students’ Chinese writing across the three cognitive stages. A total of 100 first‐year secondary students participated in three conditions: the experimental group received PBWI with GenAI chatbot support, the control group received PBWI without GenAI, and the baseline group continued product‐based instruction. Data from writing tasks, questionnaires, and interviews were analyzed using a mixed‐methods approach. Results indicated that students reported benefits of the GenAI chatbot in supporting their writing across the three cognitive stages, as well as in both lower‐ and higher‐level aspects of writing. title: The “Pressure Trap”: A Mixed‐Methods Study of the L2 Motivational Self System and Academic Achievement in a Chinese Border Region
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the relationship between the L2 motivational self system and the academic achievement of junior English majors ( N = 243) within the socio‐geographic context of a border region in Southwest China. Employing a mixed‐methods design, the research utilized questionnaires, CET‐4 scores, and semi‐structured interviews to examine how different motivational self‐guides are associated with achievement patterns. Quantitative results from correlation and multiple regression analyses indicate that while the ideal L2 self and L2 learning experience are relatively strong positive predictors of CET‐4 performance, the ought‐to L2 self is significantly but modestly negatively associated with academic performance. title: Contradiction and Construction: A Cultural‐Historical Activity Theory Analysis of a Chinese German Language Teacher's Professional Identity Formation With Generative AI
abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, challenging teachers’ professional identities. Framed by third‐generation Cultural‐Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), this case study investigates how a secondary school German teacher in China developed her professional identity through GenAI integration. Findings revealed four levels of contradictions: primary (efficiency vs. competence), secondary (AI content vs. norms; skill gaps; AI vs. creativity), tertiary (traditional vs. AI‐supported pedagogy), and quaternary (tensions with colleagues and students). Resolving these contradictions transformed her identity across four dimensions. Agentively, a reflective practitioner progressing from technology‐dependent anxiety to agentive practice. Her trajectory shifted from incremental adaptation toward emergent expansive learning. title: The Role of Positive and Negative Emotions in Resilience Among L2 Learners: A Three Level Meta‐Analytic Review
abstract: ABSTRACT Second/foreign language (L2) learning is not solely a cognitive/linguistic acquisition process but includes mixed emotional experiences. Understanding how these emotional experiences relate to resilience could help our understanding of how learners navigate fluctuations in emotions when learning an L2. This study systematically synthesizes research on the relationship between emotions and resilience in L2 learners through a three‐level meta‐analysis of 13 primary studies ( N = 5,340) published between 2019 and 2025. title: Chinese University Students’ Motivation to Learn Greek: A Transnational Postdigital Exploration
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on the motivation of learners of Languages Other Than English (LOTE) has grown steadily in recent years; however, most studies focus on classroom‐based activities and seldom consider how transnational experiences or digital practices contribute to motivational development. This study employs postdigital storytelling to qualitatively investigate how nine Chinese learners of Greek narratively construct their motivational selves throughout their Greek‐learning journeys informed by translanguaging and postdigital perspectives. Drawing on multiple data sources, including life‐history interviews, multimodal artifacts, and follow‐up interactions via email and social media, we conducted a multimodal thematic analysis to examine how LOTE motivational selves were constructed, expressed, and negotiated across digital and non‐digital linguistic activities. title: Evidence for the Development of L2 Grammar‐for‐Interaction: The Case of Wenti shi (“the Problem Is”) in L2 Chinese Interaction
abstract: ABSTRACT This study adopts an integrated framework combining Conversation Analysis for Second Language Acquisition (CA‐for‐SLA), Usage‐Based Linguistics (UBL), and Interactional Linguistics (IL) to trace the longitudinal development of an L2 Chinese learner's use of the construction wenti shi (“the problem is”, WTS) over a 15‐month period. Although quantitative analysis shows that the overall frequency of WTS did not increase substantially, qualitative findings reveal a clear developmental trajectory. Initially employed in its literal sense to present a factual problem, WTS was later mobilized to foreground an issue by upgrading the speaker's epistemic stance and projecting further talk. Building on this core function, two trajectories of functional expansion emerged: one oriented to managing topic transition and the other to prefacing contrasting stance and, eventually, disagreement. title: Take an Introductory Linguistics Course; It May Increase Your Language Learning Ability
abstract: ABSTRACT Can general linguistics knowledge be used to better learn a new language? This exploratory study is concerned with the potential advantageous transfer of general linguistics knowledge to the learning of a new, additional foreign language. We examine foreign language course letter grades (e.g., A–F) collected over 12 years at a private, predominantly STEM university in the United States. We first ask whether there is an association between taking a prior introductory linguistics class and the letter grade received in a first‐semester, beginner foreign language learning class. We indeed found a statistically significant association. Importantly, this association is seemingly unique to the linguistics course, as we found no such association between a control class (psychology) and foreign language learning letter grade. Moreover, this transfer did not work both ways. No association was found for linguistics letter grade and having taken a prior foreign language learning class.
