title: From External Schema to Internal Tool: Navigating the Semantic Labyrinth of English Modals Through CL‐Informed Concept‐Based Language Instruction
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigated to what extent and how an integrated framework of cognitive linguistics (CL) and concept‐based language instruction (CBLI) supports the acquisition of English modal verbs among L2 learners. Using a quasi‐experimental design, the study compared a CL‐CBLI group ( n = 42) with a traditional‐CBLI group ( n = 40) and a control group ( n = 40) among intermediate‐level high school learners. Data from productive accuracy tests, conceptual development measures, and concurrent verbalizations were triangulated to evaluate instructional effectiveness and the process of internalization. Results suggest that the integrated CL‐CBLI approach significantly enhanced learners’ understanding of modality, evidenced by balanced accuracy across root and epistemic functions and superior long‐term retention compared to traditional descriptive methods. These findings indicate that providing a scientifically motivated orienting basis through force dynamics allows for the development of a unified and durable cognitive tool for L2 meaning‐making.

title: EFL Learners’ Receptive Vocabulary Size and the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages: Estimates Across Levels
abstract: ABSTRACT The Common European Framework of Reference for languages (CEFR) is widely used as a reference for language teaching and learning. However, providing vocabulary size (VS) estimates is beyond the CEFR's original aim. Previous research has also shown that learners’ receptive VS is related to overall proficiency and to the four language skills. Nevertheless, the existing attempts to link receptive VS and the CEFR are very scarce and have not investigated vocabularies beyond the 5K level. The present study aims to fill these gaps by sampling 311 Spanish learners of English distributed across the six CEFR levels. title: Translanguaging, Medium of Instruction and LX Learning Motivation
abstract: ABSTRACT Multilingual education in post‐colonial societies challenges the traditional labelling of languages (e.g., L1, L2) in classroom contexts. For learners with complex linguistic repertoires, what might conventionally be called a ‘second language (L2)’ is often less a chronological L2 than an additional language (LX) that is organically integrated into the learner's repertoire and serves as a medium of learning. This recognition prompts a shift of focus from the target language promoted by the teacher to the complex processes experienced/engaged by the learner. In other words, L2 medium‐of‐instruction becomes LX medium‐of‐learning. This special issue seeks to break new paths by exploring the possibilities of this conceptual move in relation to language learning motivation (LLM). Research shows that L2 students without prior experience in L2 medium‐of‐instruction struggle with comprehension, participation and LLM, especially with demanding content. title: Edutainment Through Translanguaging Practices: A Multimodal Discourse Analysis of Short‐Form English Instructional Videos on Douyin
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent research in applied linguistics has increasingly attended to translanguaging practices in digitally mediated contexts, yet relatively little is known about how translanguaging practices achieve edutainment within the context of the highly compressed short‐form videos as dynamic discourse on Douyin, China's localized counterpart to TikTok. Drawing on translanguaging theory and multimodal discourse analysis, the study analyzes a song video and a role‐play video for English language teaching. The findings show that content creators flexibly draw on diverse multilingual and multimodal resources. The orchestration of these translanguaging resources has created unique ways for the realization of edutainment in the song video and role‐play video, respectively. The findings also indicate that the use of diverse translanguaging resources in each type of video stimulates positive emotions. title: Developing Chatbot Pragmatics Through Prompting Instruction in AI‐Assisted Communicative Practice
abstract: ABSTRACT This quasi‐experimental study examines the impact of short‐term prompting instruction on the communicative performance of Czech learners of English in human–chatbot interaction, conceptualizing their prompting behavior as a context‐specific manifestation of pragmatic competence. The study was conducted in two phases (September 2024 and May 2026) and included four groups of participants with varying chatbot experience. Participants with (experimental groups) and without (control groups) prior prompting instruction completed 20 communicative tasks of increasing complexity, during which four indicators of communication effectiveness were recorded: task completion rate, number of conversational turns, user satisfaction, and frequency of chatbot misunderstandings. title: The Multidimensional Organisation of Embodied Meaning in a Second Language
abstract: ABSTRACT Embodied cognition theories propose that conceptual knowledge is grounded in sensorimotor experience. Studies document embodied effects in second‐language (L2) processing, but the multidimensional organisation of L2 perceptual knowledge is less well understood. We examined perceptual strength and multivariate structure in L2 English. Forty‐one native Mandarin speakers rated 497 concepts in L1 Chinese, and 44 high‐proficiency Chinese–English bilinguals rated their English translations across six modalities. title: Equal Wings, Unequal Flapping: An Explanatory Sequential Mixed‐Methods Study of the Nonlinear Effect of L2 Grit on Achievement
abstract: ABSTRACT While the linear effect of second language (L2) grit on foreign language achievement is well documented, the nonlinear effect remains underexplored. To help address this gap, this explanatory sequential mixed‐methods study examined 220 rural Chinese junior high school students. Multilevel polynomial regression with response surface analysis revealed that (a) L2 achievement rose linearly when perseverance of effort (PE) and consistency of interest (CI) were congruent and increased together; (b) PE and CI appeared to play complementary roles in predicting L2 achievement; and (c) the nonlinear CI‐achievement association appeared to vary across different PE‐CI configurations. Qualitative interviews identified five themes that may help explain the observed nonlinear links: motivation, self‐efficacy, instructional context, emotions, and social support. title: Perceived Interactional Demands and Professional Role Reconceptualisation in an International Teaching Practicum
abstract: ABSTRACT International teaching practicums (ITPs) provide pre‐service teachers (PSTs) with opportunities to encounter unfamiliar linguistic, interactional and pedagogical contexts. This qualitative retrospective study examined how 17 Indonesian PSTs interpreted their experiences during an ITP in the Philippines and reconsidered language‐related, pedagogical and professional assumptions. Data comprised semi‐structured interviews, reflective blogs and lesson plans, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Transformative Learning Theory (TLT) was subsequently employed as an interpretive heuristic to examine variation in participants’ retrospective meaning‐making. Six interrelated themes showed how participants entered the practicum with idealised expectations of an ESL context, encountered perceived interactional and linguistic demands, questioned assumptions about English proficiency and language use, and adapted their pedagogical practices. title: Examining the Interaction Between Translation and Translanguaging in Proper‐name Transcreation on Chinese Social Media
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines proper‐name transcreation on Rednote, a Chinese social media platform, and explores the interaction between translation and translanguaging in this process. Drawing on Jakobson's tripartite typology of translation and Sato's translanguaging approach to translation, the study employs a mixed‐methods approach to analyze 242 valid cases and develops a three‐dimensional framework of interlingual, intralingual, and intersemiotic translanguaging, highlighting the co‐mobilization of diverse meaning‐making resources in proper‐name transcreation. The findings show that interlingual translanguaging is the most prevalent, followed by intralingual translanguaging, while intersemiotic translanguaging, which foregrounds multimodal resources, is the least frequent. The sub‐strategies within these three dimensions also display distinct distributional patterns. title: Taking a Stance: Scholar‐Written and ChatGPT‐Generated Academic Blogs
abstract: ABSTRACT The advent of Large Language Models in the last few years has dramatically changed the landscape of academic writing, not least in the domain of scientific blogging. Not only can GenAI tools draft posts quickly, but they can potentially synthesise and transform complex research articles for a blog audience of lay readers. In this way they can bridge the gap between academia and the public while at the same time assisting non‐native speakers in producing fluent academic writing. Despite this development, however, little research has systematically explored the rhetorical construction of these AI‐generated blogs and how they compare with those created by human scholars. In this paper, we explore this comparison by focusing on stance. Using Hyland's (2005) stance model, we investigate similarities and differences between scholar‐written blogs on COVID‐19 and those generated by ChatGPT‐5 from the same 100 research articles. Our findings highlight how stance functions as a key resource in the reworking of scientific knowledge for public audiences and contribute to ongoing debates about authorial voice, knowledge dissemination and accountability in AI‐generated academic writing.

title: A Comparative Study of the Pragmatic Capabilities of ChatGPT and Humans in Compliment Responses in English
abstract: ABSTRACT Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), exemplified by AI‐driven chatbots like ChatGPT, has stimulated considerable interest in the field of applied linguistics. However, important questions regarding ChatGPT's affordances for second language (L2) learning and teaching remain under‐investigated. For instance, what are ChatGPT's inherent linguistic attributes (e.g., pragmatic capabilities)? Furthermore, to what extent does ChatGPT reflect human pragmatic competence so that this AI‐driven chatbot can be leveraged as a viable tool for L2 pragmatics acquisition? To fill this gap, the current study compared ChatGPT's pragmatic capability in responding to compliments in English with that of humans. Compliment responses were collected from ChatGPT‐3.5 and 230 human participants (129 first‐language English speakers, 101 advanced L2 English speakers) through synchronous text‐based conversation tasks. title: Modelling Behavioural Pathways to L2 Listening Comprehension: L2 Listening Self‐Efficacy, L2 Listening Enjoyment and the Mediating Role of Informal Digital L2 Listening Behaviour
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite growing interest in informal digital learning of English (IDLE), less is known about how skill‐specific digital listening behaviour contributes to second language (L2) listening comprehension. Drawing on social cognitive theory, this study examined the relationships among L2 listening self‐efficacy, L2 listening enjoyment, IDLE listening behaviour and L2 listening comprehension in a Chinese English as a foreign language (EFL) context. Specifically, it investigated whether IDLE listening behaviour functions as a behavioural pathway through which listening‐related beliefs and emotions are associated with listening outcomes. Data were collected from 478 first‐year university students and analysed using structural equation modelling. The results showed that both L2 listening self‐efficacy and L2 listening enjoyment were positively associated with L2 listening comprehension, and IDLE listening behaviour significantly mediated these relationships. title: Making Ethical AI Teachable: Distributed Accountability in Language Teacher Education
abstract: ABSTRACT Discussions of ethical generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use in language education are often disconnected: whether by focusing on practical concerns (classroom dos and don'ts around disclosure, academic integrity, the boundaries of acceptable assistance) or through broader critical questions concerning surveillance, platform power, data extraction, linguistic bias and unequal participation in AI development. This split has practical consequences for language teacher education because it associates ethics with teacher compliance while leaving GenAI's structural conditions unexamined. This viewpoint article proposes distributed accountability as a conceptual and teachable framework for ethical AI praxis. It provides a language‐education‐specific framework that highlights how responsibility is shared by learners, teachers, institutions, AI developers and vendors.
